left: The dark tree and seated musicians crowd the left side.
right: The hill town and upright tower occupy the open right side.
observation: Cleveland attributes the figures and landscape to two makers. It describes the view as a constructed pastoral scene.
limit: A close view of the players cannot establish how a particular town sounded in 1517.
windowReply: The doorway group spots where the players sit. I add the landscape makers’ names beside the projected figures.
tableReply: The study reader can follow where the two hands meet. She asks for separate lines for what the engravers made and what the picture depicts.
title: Shepherds in a Landscape

makerAndPlace: Master of the Small Landscapes · Flanders
medium: pen and brown ink on paper
left: The buildings sit close together on the left side of the drawn horizon.
right: The pasture and open land extend to the right.
observation: The museum documents the connection between this ink drawing and a separately accessioned print. The publisher described the series as drawn from life.
limit: The publisher’s claim alone cannot identify the village or date a sighting of it.
windowReply: Visitors find the building line quickly. The open pasture lies beyond the lit cut, so I leave a second pointing slip beside it.
tableReply: The study group can compare the apparent route through the scene. They leave the village name blank on the finding ribbon.
title: Landscape with a Moated Village

left: Small buildings and slopes read as an outline in the left distance.
right: Pine trunks and dark plant forms interrupt the right foreground.
observation: Cleveland dates the etching to Altdorfer’s early landscape prints and treats the depicted site as potentially imagined.
limit: Recognisable trees and buildings do not locate a known site.
windowReply: The group copies the tree outline onto a shadow card. Their card keeps the artist’s name and leaves the place uncertain.
tableReply: Readers compare the distant roofs and nearer trunks. They can show how the view is organised even while the location stays open.
title: Landscape with Two Pines

dateKind: Catalogue date of this albumen print
medium: albumen print from a wet-collodion negative
left: Dense trunks and shadow frame the left side.
right: Two figures are easier to pick out on the light ground to the right of centre.
observation: The museum associates this particular print with White’s photographs in northern Wales and identifies the photographic process.
limit: A photographic process can record a scene without revealing who posed or how a photographer arranged it.
windowReply: The day reader sees bodies behind the glare. I keep a question beside the image about what the figure positions alone can tell us.
tableReply: The evening group follows the lit ground across both halves. They look for how the photograph guides the eye before assigning it a documentary job.
title: Landscape

left: Fine vertical tree lines gather toward the left.
right: Open and dark areas break up the middle and right of the grove.
observation: The museum identifies three print processes used for this view near where Pissarro lived.
limit: Granular tone can represent light without recording an actual measured light level or a specific hour.
windowReply: Children find the tree line after I move the curtain. The sketch card gives them a feature to draw when the coloured lamps change.
tableReply: Study readers compare line with tone across the grove and explain how two different kinds of mark can make a place legible.
title: Wooded Landscape at L'Hermitage, Pontoise

medium: etching and open-bite on laid paper
left: Light figures stand near the lower edge under dark trees.
right: Light columns and broken walls stand against a dark ground.
observation: The museum calls attention to the reversal in which light forms stand out on a dark field, an unusual effect for etching at the time.
limit: The print’s light-and-dark choices cannot establish the time of day at an actual ford.
windowReply: The day reader catches the pale columns through the glare. The card says who made that effect and leaves the actual light open.
tableReply: The study group can place animals and columns within the same light-dark experiment. They keep the idea of an engineered reversal beside the image.
title: Pastoral Landscape with Ruins and a Ford

dateKind: Catalogue date of this two-plate print
medium: etching from two plates on one sheet
left: The little town and river read as a whole on the left.
right: Big trees and a cottage sit close to the right edge.
observation: The sheet brings together two etching plates. The museum identifies marks in the sky from the printing process and leaves the reason for the pairing open.
limit: The fact that two plates share a sheet does not settle why they were paired or whether they depict one place.
windowReply: The window group spots the half I selected. I give them a clipped note so they know there is another plate on this sheet.
tableReply: The study reader compares the joins and keeps a separate card for the printer’s marks. They distinguish the evidence of pairing from the reason for it.
title: Landscape with the Town on a River and the Cottage between Trees

makerAndPlace: Adrian Zingg · Tharandt near Dresden, with the maker from Switzerland
dateKind: Catalogue date of this etching, distinct from the age of the ruin
left: A tree and slope frame the foreground at the left.
right: The distant rise and ruin sit beyond the flatter foreground.
observation: The museum identifies this impression as one of two Tharandt views and connects Zingg’s approach to his sketches of sites in Saxony.
limit: The date given for the print does not date the construction or decay of the building in it.
windowReply: Visitors follow the contour of the hill. I give the print its own date card so an old ruin does not make the paper seem medieval.
tableReply: Study readers compare the deliberately ordered foreground with the real site named in the source. They reserve a line for the difference between the two dates.
title: Landscape with Tharandt Castle Ruins

makerAndPlace: John Burke · Afghanistan album by an Irish photographer
dateKind: Date range attached to this album print in the catalogue
left: The receding ridges fill most of the lit distance on the left.
right: A tree and darker slope mark the edge of the view at right.
observation: Cleveland links the album to the Second Anglo-Afghan War and distinguishes scenery and infrastructure photographs from moving battle scenes.
limit: This page does not locate a battle or record an Afghan resident’s account. Its album gives the photographer’s framing and context.
windowReply: The ridge helps the doorway reader locate the open part of the print. I leave room on the guide for an account of the place from someone who lived there.
tableReply: The study table reads the date with the album's production context. They can discuss what a war archive keeps and whose account is missing.
title: Untitled (Landscape Scene)

makerAndPlace: Magdalena van de Passe, after a coastal image by Adam Willaerts · Netherlands
left: Rocky shelves and a small figure occupy the left side of the scene.
right: The high sea runs away to the right. There is an engraved line of text below.
observation: The catalogue identifies Magdalena van de Passe's adaptation of a work by Adam Willaerts. It associates the added figure and text with the biblical story of Elijah.
limit: The story text and environmental imagery do not document a specific storm or establish a historical sighting of Elijah.
windowReply: A visitor notices the lines cut for the waves. I keep the artist and scripture caption in separate brackets on the day card.
tableReply: Readers compare inherited scene, figure and text on one sheet. They keep the source artist apart from the engraver and note how the added caption can change the reading.
title: Seashore with a High Sea

dateKind: Publication date of the lithograph in the cited portfolio
left: The oak’s leaning trunk takes up most of the left and centre.
right: Smaller pale branches reach toward the gaps on the right.
observation: The museum identifies this impression as part of a multi-artist portfolio published in 1803, in the early years of lithography.
limit: This sheet cannot establish who invented the process or whether the pictured tree grew at an identifiable location.
windowReply: The morning group can copy the main fork from a small projected window. The publisher's line stays with the leaf as it goes back into the rack.
tableReply: The table leaves both tree and paper edge visible. The catalogue identifies the participating artist and portfolio separately, so readers can find this print again.
title: Specimens of Polyautography:  Landscape with an Oak Tree

dateKind: Publication date of this impression, after the artist’s death in 1788
left: Among the nearest forms at the left are the pale cattle by dark ground.
right: Branches and areas of open tone stretch across the water to the right.
observation: The museum dates publication to 1797 and identifies Gainsborough’s print methods. The artist lived from 1727 to 1788.
limit: Publication in 1797 cannot date the artist’s original drawing or the moment a real scene was witnessed.
windowReply: The visitor finds the cattle at the low window. Our day card carries ‘published 1797’ rather than merely a date beside the artist’s name.
tableReply: The table sees why an impression can enter public circulation after its maker's death. They hold the date of the artist and the date of publication on separate slotted lines.
title: Wooded Landscape with Cows beside a Pool, Figures and Cottage
